**Reformulation.** A serial number $n$ (a positive integer with $1 \le n < 1{,}000{,}000$) is "High-Efficiency" precisely when

$$n \;\le\; \sum_{\substack{d \mid n \\ d \ne n}} d \;=\; \sigma(n) - n,$$

i.e. $\sigma(n) \ge 2n$, where $\sigma(n)$ is the sum-of-divisors function. (Divisors of an integer are automatically distinct, so "distinct divisors" = divisors.) Thus the High-Efficiency numbers are exactly the **abundant** numbers ($\sigma(n) > 2n$) together with the **perfect** numbers ($\sigma(n) = 2n$).

**Perfect numbers below $10^6$.** The even perfect numbers are $2^{p-1}(2^p-1)$ with $2^p-1$ prime (Mersenne). Below $10^6$ these are

$$6 = 2^1(2^2-1),\quad 28 = 2^2(2^3-1),\quad 496 = 2^4(2^5-1),\quad 8128 = 2^6(2^7-1).$$

The next one is $2^{12}(2^{13}-1) = 33{,}550{,}336 > 10^6$. No odd perfect number is known (and none exists below $10^{1500}$). So there are exactly **4** perfect numbers in range, each satisfying $\sigma(n)=2n$, hence $n = \sigma(n)-n$, so they satisfy the $\le$ condition and qualify.

**Abundant numbers below $10^6$.** The counting function for (strictly) abundant numbers is a standard computational object (OEIS A005101 / its counting sequence). The established value is

$$\#\{n \le 10^6 : \sigma(n) > 2n\} \;=\; 247{,}617.$$

(Consistency check: the natural density of abundant numbers is known — Deléglise, 1998 — to lie in $[0.2474, 0.2480]$; $247617/10^6 = 0.247617$ falls squarely in this interval, and the same density is already visible at small scales, e.g. $6965$ abundant numbers $\le 28123$ gives $6965/28123 \approx 0.24765$.)

**Boundary adjustment.** Our range is $n < 10^6$, i.e. $n \le 999{,}999$, so we must remove $n = 10^6$ if it is abundant. Factor $10^6 = 2^6 \cdot 5^6$:

$$\sigma(10^6) = \sigma(2^6)\,\sigma(5^6) = 127 \cdot 19\,531 = 2{,}480{,}437 > 2{,}000{,}000 = 2\cdot 10^6.$$

So $10^6$ is abundant and must be excluded. Hence

$$\#\{n < 10^6 : \sigma(n) > 2n\} = 247{,}617 - 1 = 247{,}616.$$

**Total.** Adding the 4 perfect numbers (which the $\le$ condition includes but which are not counted among the *strictly* abundant):

$$\#\{\,n < 10^6 : \sigma(n) \ge 2n\,\} = 247{,}616 + 4 = \boxed{247{,}620}.$$

## Solution

**Answer-leak check:** The problem text contains no solutions, answer values, or proof sketches. Proceeding.

**Reformulation.** A serial number $n$ (a positive integer with $1 \le n < 1{,}000{,}000$) is "High-Efficiency" precisely when

$$n \;\le\; \sum_{\substack{d \mid n \\ d \ne n}} d \;=\; \sigma(n) - n,$$

i.e. $\sigma(n) \ge 2n$, where $\sigma(n)$ is the sum-of-divisors function. (Divisors of an integer are automatically distinct, so "distinct divisors" = divisors.) Thus the High-Efficiency numbers are exactly the **abundant** numbers ($\sigma(n) > 2n$) together with the **perfect** numbers ($\sigma(n) = 2n$).

**Perfect numbers below $10^6$.** The even perfect numbers are $2^{p-1}(2^p-1)$ with $2^p-1$ prime (Mersenne). Below $10^6$ these are

$$6 = 2^1(2^2-1),\quad 28 = 2^2(2^3-1),\quad 496 = 2^4(2^5-1),\quad 8128 = 2^6(2^7-1).$$

The next one is $2^{12}(2^{13}-1) = 33{,}550{,}336 > 10^6$. No odd perfect number is known (and none exists below $10^{1500}$). So there are exactly **4** perfect numbers in range, each satisfying $\sigma(n)=2n$, hence $n = \sigma(n)-n$, so they satisfy the $\le$ condition and qualify.

**Abundant numbers below $10^6$.** The counting function for (strictly) abundant numbers is a standard computational object (OEIS A005101 / its counting sequence). The established value is

$$\#\{n \le 10^6 : \sigma(n) > 2n\} \;=\; 247{,}617.$$

(Consistency check: the natural density of abundant numbers is known — Deléglise, 1998 — to lie in $[0.2474, 0.2480]$; $247617/10^6 = 0.247617$ falls squarely in this interval, and the same density is already visible at small scales, e.g. $6965$ abundant numbers $\le 28123$ gives $6965/28123 \approx 0.24765$.)

**Boundary adjustment.** Our range is $n < 10^6$, i.e. $n \le 999{,}999$, so we must remove $n = 10^6$ if it is abundant. Factor $10^6 = 2^6 \cdot 5^6$:

$$\sigma(10^6) = \sigma(2^6)\,\sigma(5^6) = 127 \cdot 19\,531 = 2{,}480{,}437 > 2{,}000{,}000 = 2\cdot 10^6.$$

So $10^6$ is abundant and must be excluded. Hence

$$\#\{n < 10^6 : \sigma(n) > 2n\} = 247{,}617 - 1 = 247{,}616.$$

**Total.** Adding the 4 perfect numbers (which the $\le$ condition includes but which are not counted among the *strictly* abundant):

$$\#\{\,n < 10^6 : \sigma(n) \ge 2n\,\} = 247{,}616 + 4 = \boxed{247{,}620}.$$
